div.head: Ps Cn for 27
div.ab: Sunt alie, preter feras foreste, bestie, que dum inter septa et sepes foreste continentur, emendationi subiacent: quales sunt capreoli, lepores et cuniculi.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 624 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)
div.ab: There are other beasts, besides the beasts of the forest, which, while they are kept within the enclosures and hedges of the forest, are subject to compensation: such as roe-deer, hares and rabbits.

note.seg: Verf. classificirt: 1. ferae forestae, uenatio, nämlich 1a. regales, im eng. Sinne 'ueneris': Hirsch [und Damwild?]; 1b. gewöhnliche, im eng. Sinne 'forestae': Eber; 2. [anderwärts warenna genannt] Reh, Hase, Kaninchen; 3. [Raubthiere] Wolf und Fuchs; 4. Pferde, Büffel, Kühe u. s. w. [namentlich Schweine]. Diese Classification entspricht dem wirklichen Recht nicht über ganz England und nicht im ganzen Mittelalter, wohl aber stück- und zeitweise; Turner p. x f.

The author classifies: 1. ferae forestae, uenatio, namely 1a. regales, in the narrower sense 'ueneris': hart [and fallow deer?]; 1b. ordinary, in the narrower sense 'forestae': boar; 2. [elsewhere called warenna] roe, hare, rabbit; 3. [beasts of prey] wolf and fox; 4. horses, buffalo, cows etc. [especially pigs]. This classification does not correspond to the actual law throughout England nor throughout the Middle Ages, but it does in places and at times; Turner p. x f.
erst 1339 sank zwar das Reh gesetzlich zur warenna, aber schon Heinrich I. verlieh Jagd auf Rehe im Gegensatz zu vorbehaltenen cerui et porci; Chron. Abingdon. II 114; Chron. Ramesei. p. 218
The roe was indeed legally reduced to warenna only in 1339, but already Henry I granted hunting of roe in contrast to the reserved cerui et porci; Chron. Abingdon. II 114; Chron. Ramesei. p. 218
der Hase zählt nur ausnahmsweise zum Forstwild; Turner p. xii. Wilhelm I. erlaubte Chertsey die Jagd auf lepores et vulpes per totam forestam; Rymer Foed. (1816) I p. 2
The hare counts as forest game only exceptionally; Turner p. xii. William I allowed Chertsey hunting of lepores et vulpes per totam forestam; Rymer, Foed. (1816) I p. 2
Hier zitierte Urk., Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 51, ward von Wilhelm II. bestätigt; ebd. n. 439
The charter cited here, Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 51, was confirmed by William II; ibid. n. 439
